name: Graduate Employment
description: Graduate employment in Iran connects university education with the availability, accessibility, and quality of work. Research identifies persistent difficulties in absorbing educated workers, while unemployment statistics capture only part of the transition from study to employment. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Graduate Employment in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s transition from university to work, including graduate unemployment, participation, skills mismatches, and evidence gaps.

content.heading: The transition from university to work
content.content:
A university qualification and a suitable job are different achievements. Iran’s experience illustrates why expanding education must be examined alongside the economy’s capacity to create work. The World Bank’s Spring 2021 assessment described longstanding problems in absorbing educated young people, rather than a difficulty confined to the pandemic. It also noted that continued education had previously delayed labour-market entry for part of the large generation born during the 1980s. This is a historical explanation of labour supply, not a description of every graduate’s experience. [s1]

The same assessment found that much of the employment expansion before the pandemic involved self-employment and very small service businesses. A rising employment total therefore did not necessarily mean a comparable expansion in stable professional positions. For graduates, whether work uses their education is a separate question from whether they count as employed. [s1]

content.heading: What unemployment figures establish
content.content:
The World Bank reported graduate unemployment of 11.8 percent in the Iranian reporting year labelled 2023/24. This is a dated national observation, not a verified rate for the research cutoff. Its discussion identifies insufficient job creation and low participation as continuing problems, especially for women, young people, and university graduates. [s2]

An unemployment rate needs its denominator. The labour force consists of people classified as employed or unemployed; it excludes people outside those categories. Consequently, graduate unemployment should not be read as the proportion of all degree holders without jobs. Someone continuing education or no longer seeking work may fall outside the labour force. [s3]

A second distinction concerns composition: the share of unemployed people who hold degrees answers a different question from the unemployment rate among graduates. Neither measure alone establishes how long a new graduate waits for work, whether the job matches the degree, or whether earnings justify the cost of education. Those questions require additional evidence.

content.heading: Skills are only one part of the explanation
content.content:
UNCTAD’s innovation-policy review identified a mismatch between education, professional training, and industry requirements. It also described weak incentives and deficient collaboration for turning scientific capabilities into commercial innovation. Read together, these findings suggest that the transition problem cannot be reduced to graduates choosing the wrong subjects: the organisation of production and demand for skilled work also matter. This is an interpretation of a historical review, not a measured allocation of causes in today’s labour market. [s4]

A fuller account would compare outcomes by qualification, subject, gender, location, and time since graduation. It would also separate finding any work from obtaining secure, adequately paid work that uses university-level skills. Until comparable evidence is assembled, a national headline should remain a starting point for understanding graduate employment rather than a verdict on the value of an individual degree.

name: Online Education
description: Iran’s pandemic response made digital teaching and educational broadcasting central to school continuity. Its experience highlights the difference between providing a platform and ensuring that learners can access, use, and benefit from it. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Online Education in Iran: Access and Learning | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore SHAD, pandemic teaching, accessibility, and privacy, with clear distinctions between platform reach and learning outcomes.

content.heading: An emergency shift in how school worked
content.content:
When pandemic closures interrupted classroom teaching, Iran used both broadcasting and internet-based education. UNESCO’s Institute for Information Technologies in Education describes televised lessons beginning in March 2020 and the Ministry of Education’s introduction of SHAD, a student education network. SHAD reproduced familiar school arrangements online: pupils joined virtual classrooms, principals organised classes, and staff monitored attendance and teaching activity. [s1]

This matters because emergency remote teaching is more than publishing lessons on a website. It relocates communication, assignments, and the routines of school into a mediated environment. Iran’s response sought continuity through an organised school network, while television offered a different delivery channel. Neither the availability of a broadcast nor access to a virtual classroom establishes how much a particular pupil learned. [s1]

content.heading: Participation requires more than a connection
content.content:
UNESCO’s account records criticism of SHAD’s technical performance and the exclusion of pupils without suitable devices or internet access. These are distinct obstacles: a household may have connectivity but no device available when a lesson takes place, while an installed application may still be difficult to use. The historical account should not be treated as a technical audit of the platform’s current version. [s1]

Disability introduces another dimension. In the publicly accessible abstract of their qualitative study, Negin Hosseini Goodrich and Abouzar Samiei argued that the pandemic shift transferred existing physical and attitudinal barriers into online education. Their study specifically addressed students with disabilities and described SHAD as inaccessible in that context. The abstract supports identifying accessibility as a serious concern; it does not provide a national prevalence estimate or establish the condition of later releases. [s2]

content.heading: Privacy is part of educational provision
content.content:
Human Rights Watch’s investigation of government-endorsed educational technology included testimony from Iranian teachers who said public-school staff were compelled to use SHAD during the pandemic. That reported lack of choice matters when assessing meaningful consent to digital systems. The report’s technical investigations were snapshots from 2021; they should not be presented as proof of how software behaves today. [s3]

A careful evaluation therefore asks separate questions about educational usefulness, accessibility, and data handling. A useful lesson does not by itself answer what information is collected, who receives it, or whether a learner can participate through an alternative channel. These are evaluation questions, not findings that every Iranian platform has the same practices. [s3]

content.heading: From emergency provision to inclusive learning
content.content:
UNICEF’s Iran education programme identifies economic and geographical barriers, shortages of ICT equipment, and pressure on schools serving refugee communities. Its stated interventions include inclusive digital learning platforms and digital textbooks for children with disabilities and refugee children. These statements document programme priorities, rather than independently measured improvements in learning. [s4]

The central distinction is between reach and educational benefit. Evaluating online education requires evidence about who participates, who is excluded, what support teachers and families need, and what learners achieve. This page’s evidence is strongest on pandemic school provision. University teaching, adult learning, and the subsequent effectiveness of blended education require further research.

name: Innovation & Business Opportunities
description: Iran’s innovation landscape combines scientific and technical capabilities with difficult conditions for commercial development. This directory distinguishes the technologies and services businesses provide from the financing, infrastructure, and institutional conditions needed to sustain them. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Innovation & Business Opportunities in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Navigate Iran’s technology and business fields, from enterprise software and financial systems to applied innovation and entrepreneurship.

content.heading: From technical capability to a working business
content.content:
Innovation becomes economically significant when knowledge can be turned into useful products, reliable services, or better ways of producing them. Iran’s experience makes the distinction between scientific capability and commercial development particularly important. UNCTAD’s historical innovation-policy review described substantial human-capital and scientific assets alongside weaknesses in incentives, competition, and collaboration directed toward market demand. Its account is evidence about the development of the innovation system, not a current census of firms. [s1]

The World Intellectual Property Organization’s 2025 profile offers a more recent, differently constructed view. It placed Iran’s innovation outputs ahead of its innovation inputs in relative international ranking. That pattern is consistent with a system producing identifiable knowledge and technology outputs despite weaker enabling conditions. It does not mean every business is productive, every research result reaches customers, or a prospective investment will succeed. [s2]

content.heading: Software foundations and financial systems
content.content:
This directory begins with distinctions that help readers follow a product from its underlying technology to its business use. Software Development Infrastructure covers the organisations and capabilities involved in building enterprise and custom applications. Core Banking concerns the central systems behind bank accounts and transactions. Banking & Financial Systems broadens that view to functions such as lending, treasury, branch operations, customer management, and control.

Electronic Payments and Financial Technology overlap, but answer different editorial questions. The payments branch follows acceptance, gateways, switches, and transaction management. Financial Technology also includes areas such as digital credit assessment, investment services, crowdfunding, and open banking—the controlled exchange of banking functions or data through interfaces. Insurance Technology follows a separate set of processes, including policy administration, risk assessment, claims, and distribution.

These are navigation boundaries for this guide. They do not imply that a provider operates in only one branch, or that the presence of a technology establishes regulatory permission, adoption, or service quality.

content.heading: Customer platforms and the systems behind them
content.content:
E-commerce and Online Services focus on the customer-facing side of digital business: selling goods, matching participants, and arranging services. Cloud Infrastructure and Software Delivery & Operations examine the supporting systems. They ask how applications are hosted, released, monitored, secured, and kept available. A marketplace interface and the operational infrastructure beneath it are related subjects, but they require different evidence.

Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, and Cybersecurity are treated as cross-cutting capabilities. Their branch pages distinguish language and speech technologies, predictive analysis, business intelligence, identity management, and security controls. The useful editorial question is what a system demonstrably does for its users. A product description alone cannot establish accuracy, robustness, or operational effectiveness.

Blockchain Technology likewise separates infrastructure, custody, wallets, monitoring, and smart contracts. Inclusion in the taxonomy is a way to explain these activities; it is not an endorsement of particular assets or a statement about their legal treatment.

content.heading: Applied technology across economic sectors
content.content:
The applied branches organise technology around the problems it is intended to address. Health Technology follows clinical information and service administration. Education Technology covers learning delivery and assessment. Agricultural Technology includes monitoring, irrigation management, and supply chains, while Industrial Technology examines production systems and automation. Transport Technology follows fleets, routing, freight, and logistics.

Gaming & Digital Entertainment introduces another kind of product: interactive cultural and entertainment experiences. Emerging Businesses groups developing approaches such as business-process automation, specialist marketplaces, and subscription services. Across these fields, the distinction between an announced capability, a deployed system, and a measured outcome remains essential.

Entrepreneurship & Investment explains mechanisms for establishing and financing businesses. Technology Exports asks how products and technical services reach customers beyond Iran. These branches complement the sector pages rather than substituting for evidence about individual companies.

content.heading: Why operating conditions matter
content.content:
Technology does not remove the economic conditions under which a business operates. The World Bank’s Spring 2024 assessment identified sanctions, energy shortages, liquidity constraints, underinvestment, and uncertainty as impediments to non-oil activity. It also described banking restrictions and trade barriers as obstacles to technology transfer and competitiveness. These are dated findings; the report’s forecasts should not be read as observed outcomes at this page’s cutoff. [s3]

UNCTAD’s earlier diagnosis also emphasised the gap between scientific strengths and demand-led commercial innovation. Together, these sources support looking beyond the supply of engineers or the number of research outputs. They do not establish the relative importance of each constraint for a particular business today. [s1]

Regional generalisations require similar care. A national innovation profile cannot establish that firms in different cities have equivalent access to finance, specialist workers, infrastructure, or customers. This draft does not yet contain a verified regional comparison.

content.heading: What an innovation index can show
content.content:
WIPO’s 2025 country profile grouped indicators into innovation inputs and outputs, while explicitly warning that data availability and changes to its framework affect year-to-year ranking comparisons. The historical positions are therefore retained in a table rather than presented as a continuous measure of business opportunity. A change in rank is not a percentage change in innovative capacity. [s2]

WIPO’s subsequently updated country page contains a 2026 edition. It is listed as a research lead, but its release date relative to this page’s cutoff was not established during inspection, so its results are excluded here. [s4]

For readers exploring the directory, the strongest approach is to move from a defined activity to inspected evidence: what is offered, who uses it, how performance is measured, and which limitations remain. The branches provide that structure; company-specific opportunities still require current research.
